¶
'''bent-grass''' (bent′grȧs), ''n.'' Same as ''bent''<sup>2</sup>, 1.

'''benthal''' (ben′thal), ''a.'' [< Gr. βένθος, the depths of the sea, + ''-al.''] Of or pertaining to depths of the sea of a thousand fathoms and more. See extract.
{{smaller block|In his presidential address to the biological section of the British Association at Plymouth in 1877, Mr. Gwyn Jeffreys suggested the use of the name “''benthal'' . . . for depths of one thousand fathoms and more,” while retaining the term “abyssal” for depths down to one thousand fathoms.
{{right|''P. H. Carpenter'', in Science, IV. 223.}}}}

'''Benthamic''' (ben-tham′ik), ''a.'' Of or pertaining to Jeremy Bentham or to his system. See ''Benthamism''.
{{smaller block|The ''Benthamic'' standard of the greatest happiness was that which I had always been taught to apply.
{{right|''J. S. Mill'', Autobiog., p. 64.}}}}

'''Benthamism''' (ben′tham-izm), ''n.'' [< ''Bentham'' + ''-ism.''] The political and ethical system taught by Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832), who held that the greatest happiness of the greatest number is the rational end of moral rules, and ought to be the aim of governments and individuals alike; utilitarianism (which see).
{{smaller block|My previous education [that is, before 1821–2] had been, in a certain sense, already a course of ''Benthamism.''
{{right|''J. S. Mill'', Autobiog., p. 64.}}
Is ''Benthamism'' so absolutely the truth, that the Pope is to be denounced because he has not yet become a convert to it?
{{right|''J. H. Newman'', Letters (1875), p. 114.}}}}

'''Benthamite''' (ben′tham-īt), ''n.'' [< ''Bentham'' + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] A follower of Bentham; a believer in Benthamism; an adherent of the Benthamic

philosophy.
{{smaller block|A faithful ''Benthamite'' traversing an age still dimmed by the mists of transcendentalism.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Essays in Criticism, p. 13.}}}}

¶
'''bentinck''' (ben′tingk), ''n.'' [From Captain ''Bentinck'' (1737–75), the inventor.] ''Naut.'', a triangular course, used as a trysail: now generally superseded by the storm-staysail.—{{smaller|'''Bentinck boom''', a small boom on the foot of a square foresail.—'''Bentinck shrouds''', ropes extending from the weather futtock-staff to the lee-channels, to support the mast when the ship is rolling heavily. [No longer used.]}}

'''bentiness''' (ben′ti-nes), ''n.'' The state of being benty.

'''benting''' (ben′ting), ''n.'' [< ''bent''<sup>2</sup> + ''-ing''.] The act of seeking or collecting bents or bent-stalks.
{{smaller block|<poem>The pigeon never knoweth woe
Until she doth a ''benting'' go. ''Ray’s Proverbs.''</poem>}}

'''benting-time''' (ben′ting-tīm), ''n.'' The time when pigeons feed on bents before peas are ripe: as, “rare ''benting-times'',” ''Dryden'', Hind and Panther, iii. 1283.

'''bentivi, bentiveo''' (ben-tē′vē, -tẹ̄-vā′ọ̄), ''n.'' [Said to be Braz.] A name, said to be used in Brazil, of a clamatorial passerine bird of the family ''Tyrannidæ'', the ''Pitangus sulphuratus'' of authors in general, ''Tyrannus sulphuratus'' (Vieillot), ''Lanius sulphuratus'' (Linnæus), originally described in 1760 by Brisson as ''la pie-griesche jaune de Cayenne'', and hence long supposed to be a shrike.

'''ben trovato''' (bān trō-vä′tō). [It.: ''ben'', < L. ''bene'', well; ''trovato'' (pl. ''trovati''), pp. of ''trovare'', find, invent: see ''trove''.] Well feigned; well in-
readings.c1s3:
vented: a part of a familiar Italian saying, ''Se non è vero, è ben trovato'' (If it is not true, it is well imagined), sometimes introduced, in various relations, in English.

{{smaller block|Various anecdotes of him [Dante] are related by Boccaccio, Sacchetti, and others, none of them verisimilar, and some of them at least fifteen centuries old when revamped. Most of them are neither veri nor ''ben trovati.''
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 19.}}}}

'''benty''' (ben′ti), ''a.'' [< ''bent''<sup>2</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' Of, pertaining to, or of the nature of bent or bent-grass.—'''2.''' Covered with or abounding in bent.

'''benum†''', ''p. a.'' and ''v. t.'' An earlier form of ''benumb.''

'''benumb†''', '''benome<sup>1</sup>†''', ''p. a.'' [Early mod. E., < ME. ''benome, benomen,'' < AS. ''benumen,'' pp. of ''beniman,'' deprive: see ''benim.''] Benumbed.

'''benumb''' (bē̤-num′), ''v. t.'' [Early mod. E. ''benum, benombe, benome,'' < ''benumb, benum, benome,'' p. a.: see ''benumb, p. a.''] '''1.''' To make torpid; deprive of sensation: as, a hand or foot ''benumbed'' by cold.—'''2.''' To stupefy; render inactive.

{{smaller block|It seizes upon the vitals, and ''benumbs'' the senses. {{right|''South.''}}

My mind revolts at the reverence for foreign authors, which stifles inquiry, restrains investigation, ''benumbs'' the vigor of the intellectual faculties, subdues and debases the mind.
{{right|''N. Webster'', in Scudder, p. 230.}}}}

'''benumbed''' (bē̤-numd′), ''p. a.'' Numb or torpid, either physically or morally: as, ''benumbed'' limbs; ''benumbed'' faith.

'''benumbedness''' (bē-numd′nes), ''n.'' [< ''benumbed'', pp. of ''benumb'', + ''-ness''.] The state of being benumbed; absence of sensation or feeling.

'''benumbment''' (bē-num′ment), ''n.'' [< ''benumb'' + ''-ment''.] The act of benumbing; the state of being benumbed; torpor.

'''benweed''' (ben′wēd), ''n.'' [Also ''bin-'', ''bind-'', ''bunweed''; < ''ben'' (uncertain) + ''weed''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''bendwith'', ''bindweed''.] Ragwort. [Scotland and North. Ireland.]

'''benzaldehyde''' (ben-zal′dē-hīd), ''n.'' [< ''benz(oic)'' + ''aldehyde''.] The oil of bitter almonds, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COH, a colorless liquid having a pleasant odor and soluble in water. {{smaller|It is prepared artificially on a large scale, and used in making benzoic acid as well as various pigments.}}

'''benzamide''' (ben′za-mịd or -mīd), ''n.'' [< ''benz(oic)'' + ''amide''.] A white crystalline substance, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>.CO.NH<sub>2</sub>, which may be regarded as the amide of benzoyl.

'''benzene''' (ben′zēn), ''n.'' [< ''benz(oic)'' + ''-ene''.] '''1.''' A hydrocarbon (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) formed whenever organic bodies are subjected to destructive distillation at a high temperature, and obtained commercially from coal-tar. {{smaller|It is a clear, colorless liquid, of a peculiar ethereal, agreeable odor, used in the arts as a solvent for gums, resins, fats, etc., and as the material from which aniline and the aniline colors are derived. Also called ''benzol'', ''benzolin''.}}

'''2.''' Same as ''benzin'' or ''benzine''.

'''benzil''' (ben′zil), ''n.'' [< ''benz(oin)'' + ''-il''.] A compound (C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) obtained by the oxidation of benzoin, and also by heating bromotoluylene with water at 150° C.

'''benzoin''' (ben′zō-in or -zoin), ''n.'' [First in 16th century; also written ''benjoin'', ''bengewyne'', ''bengwin'', later ''benzion'', etc. (also corruptly ''benjamin''<sup>2</sup>, q. v.), = D. ''benjuin'' = G. ''benzoe'', ''benzoin'' = Dan. ''benzoe'', < F. ''benjoin'', < Pg. ''beijoim'' = Sp. ''benjuí'', ''menjuí'' = It. ''benzoi'', < Ar. ''lubān jāwa'', lit. ‘incense of Java’ (Sumatra). The omission in Rom. of the syllable ''lu-'' was prob. due to its being mistaken for the def. art.] Gum benjamin; the concrete resinous juice of ''Styrax Benzoin'', a tree of Sumatra, Java, and the Malay peninsula, obtained by incisions into the bark. {{smaller|The benzoin of commerce is obtained from both Sumatra and Siam, that from Siam being much superior to the other in quality. When rubbed or heated, it has a fragrant and agreeable odor. It is chiefly used in cosmetics and perfumes, and in incense in Roman Catholic and Greek churches, and is the base of the tincture called ''friars’'' or ''Turlington’s balsam'', long famous as a remedy for bronchitis and an effective application to indolent sores, etc. It forms the medicinal ingredient of court-plaster. See ''Styrax''.}}

'''benzol''' (ben′zol), ''n.'' [Less prop. ''benzole''; < ''benz''(''oic'') + ''-ol''.] Same as ''benzene'', 1.

'''benzolin''' (ben′zō-lin), ''n.'' [< ''benzol'' + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.] Same as ''benzene'', 1.

'''benzolize''' (ben′zō-līz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''benzolized'', ppr. ''benzolizing''. [< ''benzol'' + ''-ize''.] To treat, impregnate, or cause to combine with benzene or a benzene derivative.

'''benzoyl''' (ben′zō-il or -zoil), ''n.'' [< ''benzo''(''ic'') + ''-yl''.] The radical (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O) of benzoic acid, of oil of bitter almonds, and of an extensive series of compounds derived from this oil, or connected with it by certain relations.

'''benzyl''' (ben′zil), ''n.'' [< ''benz(oic)'' + ''-yl.''] An organic radical (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>) which does not exist in the free state, but in combination forms a considerable number of compounds.

'''benzylation''' (ben-zi-lā′shọn), ''n.'' [< ''benzyl'' + ''-ation.''] The act of adding benzene to rosaniline or some similar substance.
{{smaller block|The tendency of the ''benzylation'' being to give the colour a bluer shade.
{{right|''Crace-Calvert'', Dyeing and Calico-printing, p. 399.}}}}

'''benzylic''' (ben-zil′ik), ''a.'' [< ''benzyl'' + ''-ic.''] Related to or containing the radical benzyl.

'''bepaint''' (bē-pānt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''paint.''] To paint; cover with paint, or as with paint.
{{smaller block|Else would a maiden blush ''bepaint'' my cheek.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 2.}}}}

'''bepale''' (bē-pāl′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pale''<sup>2</sup>.] To make pale.
{{smaller block|Those perjur’d lips of thine, ''bepaled'' with blasting sighs.
{{right|''Carew'', To an Inconstant Servant.}}}}

'''bepat''' (bē-pat′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bepatted'', ppr. ''bepatting.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pat.''] To beat upon; patter upon.
{{smaller block|<poem>As timing well the equal sound
Thy clutching feet ''bepat'' the ground.</poem>
{{right|''J. Baillie'', The Kitten.}}}}

'''bepearl''' (bē-pėrl′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pearl.''] To cover with pearls, or with shining drops like pearls.
{{smaller block|This primrose all ''bepearled'' with dew.
{{right|''Carew'', The Primrose.}}}}

'''bepelt''' (bē-pelt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pelt''<sup>1</sup>.] To pelt

'''benzolin''' (ben′zō-lin), ''n.''   [< ''benzol'' + ''-in''<sup>2</sup>.]   Same as ''benzene'', 1.

'''benzolize''' (ben′zō-līz), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''benzolized'', ppr. ''benzolizing''.   [< ''benzol'' + ''-ize''.]   To treat, impregnate, or cause to combine with benzene or a benzene derivative.

'''benzoyl''' (ben′zō-il or -zoil), ''n.''   [< ''benzo''(''ic'') + ''-yl''.]   The radical (C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O) of benzoic acid, of oil of bitter almonds, and of an extensive series of compounds derived from this oil, or connected with it by certain relations.

'''benzyl''' (ben′zil), ''n.''   [< ''benz(oic)'' + ''-yl.'']   An organic radical (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>) which does not exist in the free state, but in combination forms a considerable number of compounds.

'''benzylation''' (ben-zi-lā′shọn), ''n.''   [< ''benzyl'' + ''-ation.'']   The act of adding benzene to rosaniline or some similar substance.
{{smaller block|The tendency of the ''benzylation'' being to give the colour a bluer shade.
{{right|''Crace-Calvert'', Dyeing and Calico-printing, p. 399.}}}}

'''benzylic''' (ben-zil′ik), ''a.''   [< ''benzyl'' + ''-ic.'']   Related to or containing the radical benzyl.

'''bepaint''' (bē-pānt′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''paint.'']   To paint; cover with paint, or as with paint.
{{smaller block|Else would a maiden blush ''bepaint'' my cheek.
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 2.}}}}

'''bepale''' (bē-pāl′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pale''<sup>2</sup>.]   To make pale.
{{smaller block|Those perjur’d lips of thine, ''bepaled'' with blasting sighs.
{{right|''Carew'', To an Inconstant Servant.}}}}

'''bepat''' (bē-pat′), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bepatted'', ppr. ''bepatting.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pat.'']   To beat upon; patter upon.
{{smaller block|<poem>As timing well the equal sound
Thy clutching feet ''bepat'' the ground.</poem>
{{right|''J. Baillie'', The Kitten.}}}}

'''bepearl''' (bē-pėrl′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pearl.'']   To cover with pearls, or with shining drops like pearls.
{{smaller block|This primrose all ''bepearled'' with dew.
{{right|''Carew'', The Primrose.}}}}

'''bepelt''' (bē-pelt′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pelt''<sup>1</sup>.]   To pelt soundly.

'''bepepper''' (bẹ̄-pep′ėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pepper.'']   To pepper; pelt with thickly falling blows.

'''bepester''' (bẹ̄-pes′tėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pester.'']   To pester greatly; plague; harass.

'''bepinch''' (bẹ̄-pinch′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pinch.'']   To pinch or bruise all over.
{{smaller block|<poem>In their sides, arms, shoulders, all ''bepincht'',
Ran thick the weals.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xxiii.}}}}

'''bepink†''' (bẹ̄-pingk′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pink.'']   To pink; cut in scallops or pierce with small holes.

'''bepiss''' (bẹ̄-pis′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''piss.'']   To piss upon; wet with urine.

'''bepitch†''' (bẹ̄-pich′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pitch''<sup>2</sup>.]   To cover or stain with pitch; hence, to blacken or darken.   ''Sylvester.''

'''bepity''' (bẹ̄-pit′i), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bepitied'', ppr. ''bepitying.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pity.'']   To pity exceedingly.
{{smaller block|Mercy on him, poor heart! I ''bepitied'' him, so I did.
{{right|''Fielding'', Tom Jones, x. 9.}}}}

'''beplait''' (bẹ̄-plāt′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''plait.'']   To plait.

'''beplaster''' (bẹ̄-plȧs′tėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''plaster.'']   To cover with plaster; cover or smear over thickly; bedaub.
{{smaller block|''Beplaster’d'' with rouge.{{right|''Goldsmith'', Retaliation.}}}}

'''beplume''' (bẹ̄-plöm′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''plume.'']   To furnish or adorn with feathers; plume.

'''bepommel''' (bẹ̄-pum′el), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pommel.'']   To pommel soundly; drub.

'''bepowder''' (bẹ̄-pou′dėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''powder.'']   To powder; sprinkle or cover all over with powder, as the hair.
{{smaller block|Is the beau compelled against his will to . . . employ . . . all the thought withinside his noddle to ''bepowder'' and becurl the outside?{{right|''A. Tucker'', Freewill, Foreknowledge, etc., p. 98.}}}}

'''bepraise''' (bẹ̄-prāz′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''praise.'']   To praise greatly or extravagantly; puff.
{{smaller block|''Bepraised'' by newspapers and magazines.{{right|''Goldsmith'', Essays, viii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Hardly any man, and certainly no politician, has been so ''bepraised'' as Burke.{{right|''Contemporary Rev.'', L. 27.}}}}

'''bepray''' (bẹ̄-prā′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pray.'']   To pray; beseech.   ''Shak.''

'''beprose''' (bẹ̄-prōz′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''prose.'']   To reduce to prose.
{{smaller block|To ''beprose'' all rhyme.{{right|''Mallet'', Verbal Criticism.}}}}

'''bepucker''' (bẹ̄-puk′ėr), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''pucker.'']   To pucker.

'''bepuff''' (bẹ̄-puf′), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''puff.'']   To puff; bepraise.
{{smaller block|Doggeries never so diplomaed, ''bepuffed'', gaslighted, continue doggeries.{{right|''Carlyle'', Past and Present, p. 392.}}}}

'''bepurple''' (bē-pėr′pl), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''purple.'']   To tinge or dye with a purple color.   ''Digges.''

'''bepuzzle''' (bē-puz′l), ''v. t.''   [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''puzzle.'']   To puzzle greatly; perplex.

'''bepuzzlement''' (bē-puz′l-mẹnt), ''n.''   [< ''bepuzzle'' + ''-ment.'']   Perplexity.

'''bequeath''' (bē-kwēᴛ̵ʜ′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''bequethen'', ''biquethen'', earlier ''bicwethen'', < AS. ''becwethan'', declare, affirm, give by will, < ''be-'' + ''cwethan'', say. The simple verb became obsolete in the ME. period, except in the pret. ''quoth'', which<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
